newsitem.title: USA: Republicans seek Bosnia perjury investigation.
newsitem.headline: Republicans seek Bosnia perjury investigation.

text.p: House Republicans have asked for an investigation into whether U.S. officials lied to Congress about the Clinton administration's position on Iran's 1994 arming of Bosnian forces, according to a letter obtained on Tuesday.

The letter from Republicans on a special House of Representatives investigative subcommittee asks Attorney General Janet Reno to check whether the officials, including the nominee for CIA Director, Anthony Lake, committed perjury.
The letter was sent last year but only recently declassified. A copy was given to Reuters.

The subcommittee plans to release on Friday or Monday a declassified version of its final report on the U.S. policy toward Iran's arming of Bosnian forces, and congressional sources said it will criticise Lake.
A Justice Department spokesman would not say on Tuesday if Reno had agreed to investigate Lake and other officials or had rejected the request.
He said "the letter has been received and reviewed" but would make no further comment.
The subcommittee's senior Democrat, Lee Hamilton of Indiana, issued a statement saying there was no perjury or any other criminal wrongdoing.

"The allegations that some officials may have lied to Congress are grounded solely on discrepancies among the testimony of various officials who are seeking to recall details of conversations, meetings and even facial expressions in meetings that took place two-and-a-half years ago," Hamilton said.
But Republican members still want Reno to investigate several possible cases of perjury, including contradictory testimony by Lake and other officials about his instructions to U.S. diplomats.

Senate critics have said they will challenge Lake's handling of the Iran-Bosnia policy at his Senate confirmation hearing on becoming the Central Intelligence Agency's director, set to begin next month.

Administration officials have said President Bill Clinton approved U.S. policy in 1994 not to oppose Croatian plans to transship Iranian arms to Bosnian government forces despite the U.N. arms embargo at the time.
They said U.S. diplomats were ordered to tell Croatian officials they had "no instructions" on what to say about the Iranian arms shipments.
But the Republican letter told Reno there was contradictory testimony by Lake and other officials on how far he told the U.S. diplomats to go.

They quoted the two diplomats, U.S. Ambassador to Croatia Peter Galbraith and then special U.S. envoy Charles Redman, as saying a Lake aide told them Lake's instructions were said "with a raised eyebrow."
The Republicans quoted the diplomats as saying the raised eyebrow meant they should make clear to Croatia that Washington did not oppose the Iranian arms.

The Republicans quoted Lake and the aide as saying first that the "no instructions" instructions were given to the two diplomats by the State Department, not Lake, and second that Lake made clear the diplomats were not to go beyond the "no instructions" policy.
The Republicans asked Reno to investigate whether the contradition amounted to criminal conspiracy and obstruction of Congress as well as perjury.
